title: Temurah 3
description: Whether a Jew can substitute for an animal a gentile consecrated for him, the sources for each of the baraita’s rulings on offerings consecrated by gentiles, and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili’s list of those flogged even for a prohibition that involves no action: the oath, the substitution and the curse using God’s name.
topics: ❓ A gentile consecrates, a Jew atones: must the animal be in a substituter’s hands from start to finish? Teiku
📜 Gentiles’ offerings: no misuse, piggul, notar or impurity, each derived by verbal analogy
🍷 Libations for a gentile’s burnt offering, Rabbi Yosei’s stringency, and Temple-maintenance property
⚖️ Rav: no lashes for a prohibition without an action, so the mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda on one point
🗣️ Rabbi Yosei HaGelili’s exceptions: the oath, the substitution and the curse using the Name
🤥 Which false oath earns lashes: “I ate” and “I did not eat,” and the two clauses of the mishna in Shevuot
✋ “Then the Lord will make your plagues wondrous”: lashes for one who curses another using the Name

a1.he: עַל שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ — טוֹבַת הֲנָאָה שֶׁלּוֹ!

a2.he: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָתָם הוּא דְּקָאָתֵי מִכֹּחַ יִשְׂרָאֵל, מִשּׁוּם הָכִי אָזְלִינַן בָּתַר מִתְכַּפֵּר, וְהָוֵה לֵיהּ תְּחִילָּתוֹ וְסוֹפוֹ בְּיַד יִשְׂרָאֵל. אֲבָל הָכָא, הָכִי קָא מִיבַּעְיָא לֵיהּ: מִי בָּעֵינַן מִתְּחִילָּה וְעַד סוֹף דְּתֵיקוּ בִּרְשׁוּת מַאן דְּעָבֵיד תְּמוּרָה? תֵּיקוּ.

a3.he: אָמַר מָר: מוּקְדְּשֵׁי גּוֹיִם לֹא נֶהֱנִין וְלֹא מוֹעֲלִין. לֹא נֶהֱנִין — מִדְּרַבָּנַן, וְלֹא מוֹעֲלִין — מִדְּאוֹרָיְיתָא.

a4.he: מַאי טַעְמָא? דִּכְתִיב: ״נֶפֶשׁ כִּי תִּמְעֹל מַעַל וְחָטְאָה בִּשְׁגָגָה״, וְיָלְפִינַן ״חֵטְא״ ״חֵטְא״ מִתְּרוּמָה, וּבִתְרוּמָה כְּתִיב: ״בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל״, וְלֹא גּוֹיִם.

a5.he: וְאֵין חַיָּיבִין עֲלֵיהֶם, מִשּׁוּם פִּיגּוּל, נוֹתָר, וְטָמֵא, דִּכְתִיב בַּהּ בְּטוּמְאָה: ״דַּבֵּר אֶל אַהֲרֹן וְאֶל בָּנָיו וְיִנָּזְרוּ מִקׇּדְשֵׁי בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְלֹא יְחַלְּלוּ אֶת שֵׁם וְגוֹ׳״.

a6.he: וְיָלֵיף נוֹתָר ״חִילּוּל״ ״חִילּוּל״ מִטּוּמְאָה, דִּכְתִיב גַּבֵּי טוּמְאָה: ״בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְלֹא יְחַלְּלוּוְגוֹ׳״, וּכְתִיב גַּבֵּי נוֹתָר: ״וְאוֹכְלָיו עֲוֹנוֹ יִשָּׂא כִּי אֶת קֹדֶשׁ ה׳ חִלֵּל״.

a7.he: וְיָלֵיף פִּיגּוּל ״עָוֹן״ ״עָוֹן״ מִנּוֹתָר, דִּכְתִיב גַּבֵּי פִּיגּוּל: ״וְהַנֶּפֶשׁ הָאוֹכֶלֶת מִמֶּנּוּ עֲוֹנָהּ תִּשָּׂא״, וּכְתִיב גַּבֵּי נוֹתָר: ״וְאוֹכְלָיו עֲוֹנוֹ יִשָּׂא כִּי אֶת קֹדֶשׁ ה׳ חִלֵּל״, וְכוּלְּהוּ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְלֹא גּוֹיִם.

a8.he: וְאֵין עוֹשִׂין תְּמוּרָה, דִּכְתִיב: ״לֹא יַחֲלִיפֶנּוּ וְלֹא יָמִיר״, וּכְתִיב בְּרֵישׁ עִנְיָן: ״דַּבֵּר אֶל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לֵאמֹר אִישׁ כִּי יַפְלִיא נֶדֶר בְּעֶרְכְּךָ״.

a9.he: לִישָּׁנָא אַחֲרִינָא: וְאֵין עוֹשִׂין תְּמוּרָה, מַאי טַעְמָא? דְּאִיתַּקַּשָׁא תְּמוּרַת בְּהֵמָה לְמַעְשַׂר בְּהֵמָה, וּמַעְשַׂר בְּהֵמָה לְמַעֲשֵׂר דָּגָן. וְגַבֵּי מַעְשַׂר דָּגָן כְּתִיב: ״(כֹּל) [כִּי אֶת] מַעְשַׂר בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲשֶׁר יָרִימוּ לַה׳... בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל״ — וְלֹא גּוֹיִם.

a10.he: וְאֵין מֵבִיא (עֲלֵיהֶן) נְסָכִים, אֲבָל קׇרְבָּנוֹ טָעוּן נְסָכִים, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן. מְנָא הָנֵי מִילֵּי? דְּתָנוּ רַבָּנַן: ״אֶזְרָח״ — אֶזְרָח מֵבִיא נְסָכִים וְאֵין הַגּוֹי מֵבִיא נְסָכִים. יָכוֹל לֹא תְּהֵא עוֹלָתוֹ טְעוּנָה נְסָכִים? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר ״כָּכָה״.

a11.he: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי: רוֹאֶה אֲנִי בְּכוּלָּן לְהַחְמִיר. מַאי טַעְמָא? ״לַה׳״ כְּתִיב בֵּיהּ.

a12.he: בַּמֶּה דְּבָרִים אֲמוּרִים — בְּקׇדְשֵׁי מִזְבֵּחַ, אֲבָל בְּקׇדְשֵׁי בֶּדֶק הַבַּיִת — מוֹעֲלִין בָּהֶן. מַאי טַעְמָא? דְּכִי גָּמְרִינַן מְעִילָה ״חֵטְא״ ״חֵטְא״ מִתְּרוּמָה, דֻּומְיָא דִּתְרוּמָה (דקדוש) [דִּקְדוֹשָׁה] קְדוּשַּׁת הַגּוּף, אֲבָל בקדשי בֶּדֶק הַבַּיִת דִּקְדוּשַּׁת דָּמִים — לָא.

a13.he: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה, אָמַר רַב: כׇּל ״לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה״ בַּתּוֹרָה, עָשָׂה (בָּהּ) מַעֲשֶׂה — חַיָּיב, לֹא עָשָׂה (בָּהּ) מַעֲשֶׂה — פָּטוּר.

a14.he: וּכְלָלָא הוּא דְּלָאו שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה פָּטוּר? וַהֲרֵי מֵימֵר, דְּלָאו שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה הוּא, וְלָקֵי, דִּתְנַן: ״לֹא שֶׁהוּא רַשַּׁאי לְהָמִיר, אֶלָּא שֶׁאִם הֵמִיר מוּמָר, וְסוֹפֵג אֶת הָאַרְבָּעִים״.

a15.he: אָמַר לְךָ רַב: הָא מַנִּי? רַבִּי יְהוּדָה הִיא, דְּאָמַר: לָאו שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה — לוֹקִין עָלָיו.

a16.he: וּמִי מָצֵית מוֹקְמַתְּ לְמַתְנִיתִין כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה? וְהָא אוֹקֵימְתַּאּ לְרֵישָׁא דְּלָא כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה, דְּקָתָנֵי ״הַכֹּל מְמִירִין״, ״הַכֹּל״ לְאֵיתוֹיֵי מַאי? לְאֵיתוֹיֵי יוֹרֵשׁ, וּדְלָא כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה!

a17.he: הַאי תַּנָּא סָבַר לַהּ כְּוָותֵיהּ בַּחֲדָא — דְּלָאו שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה לוֹקִין עָלָיו, וּפְלִיג עֲלֵיהּ בַּחֲדָא — דְּאִילּוּ רַבִּי יְהוּדָה סָבַר: יוֹרֵשׁ אֵינוֹ סוֹמֵךְ, יוֹרֵשׁ אֵינוֹ מֵמִיר, וְתַנָּא דִידַן סָבַר: יוֹרֵשׁ סוֹמֵךְ, יוֹרֵשׁ מֵמִיר.

a18.he: אָמַר רַב אִידִי בַּר אָבִין, אָמַר רַב עַמְרָם, אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק, אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַגְּלִילִי: כׇּל לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה, עָשָׂה בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה — לוֹקֶה, לֹא עָשָׂה בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה — פָּטוּר, חוּץ מִנִּשְׁבָּע, וּמֵימֵר, וּמְקַלֵּל חֲבֵירוֹ בַּשֵּׁם, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא עָשָׂה מַעֲשֶׂה — חַיָּיב. מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא אָמְרוּ: אַף הַמַּקְדִּים תְּרוּמָה לְבִיכּוּרִים.

a19.he: נִשְׁבָּע מְנָלַן? אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי מֵאִיר: אָמַר קְרָא ״כִּי לֹא יְנַקֶּה ה׳ אֵת אֲשֶׁר יִשָּׂא אֶת שְׁמוֹ לַשָּׁוְא״, בֵּית דִּין שֶׁל מַעְלָה

b1.he: אֵין מְנַקִּין אוֹתוֹ, אֲבָל בֵּית דִּין שֶׁל מַטָּה מַלְקִין אוֹתוֹ וּמְנַקִּין אוֹתוֹ.

b2.he: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב פָּפָּא לְאַבָּיֵי: וְאֵימָא לָא תִּיהְוֵי לֵיהּ נְקִיּוּת כְּלָל! אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִם כֵּן, לִכְתּוֹב קְרָא ״לֹא יִנָּקֶה״ וְלִישְׁתּוֹק, ״ה׳״ לְמָה לִי? בֵּית דִּין שֶׁל מַעְלָה הוּא דְּאֵין מְנַקִּין אוֹתוֹ, אֲבָל בֵּית דִּין שֶׁל מַטָּה מַלְקִין וּמְנַקִּין אוֹתוֹ.

b3.he: אַשְׁכְּחַן שְׁבוּעַת שָׁוְא, שְׁבוּעַת שֶׁקֶר מְנָלַן? רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן דִּידֵיהּ אָמַר: ״לַשָּׁוְא״ ״לַשָּׁוְא״ שְׁנֵי פְּעָמִים, אִם אֵינוֹ עִנְיָן לִשְׁבוּעַת שָׁוְא — תְּנֵיהוּ עִנְיָן לִשְׁבוּעַת שֶׁקֶר, דְּלוֹקֶה.

b4.he: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ: שְׁבוּעַת שֶׁקֶר הֵיכִי דָּמֵי? אִי נֵימָא דַּאֲמַר ״שֶׁלֹּא אוֹכַל״ וַאֲכַל — הָתָם (הוּא) מַעֲשֵׂה עֲבַד, וְאֶלָּא דְּאָמַר ״שֶׁאוֹכַל״ וְלָא אֲכַל — הָהוּא מִי לָקֵי? וְהָאִיתְּמַר: ״שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁאוֹכַל כִּכָּר זֶה הַיּוֹם״ וְעָבַר הַיּוֹם וְלֹא אָכַל — רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ אָמְרִי: אֵינוֹ לוֹקֶה.

b5.he: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אוֹמֵר: אֵינוֹ לוֹקֶה, דְּלָאו שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה הוּא, וְכׇל לָאו שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה אֵין לוֹקִין עָלָיו. וְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אָמַר: אֵינוֹ לוֹקֶה, מִשּׁוּם דְּהָוֵה לֵיהּ הַתְרָאַת סָפֵק, וְכׇל הַתְרָאַת סָפֵק אֵין לוֹקִין עָלָיו!

b6.he: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ: תְּהֵא בְּ״אָכַלְתִּי״ וְ״לֹא אָכַלְתִּי״.

b7.he: וּמַאי שְׁנָא דְּקָא מְרַבֵּה ״אָכַלְתִּי״ וְ״לֹא אָכַלְתִּי״ מֵ״אוֹכַל״ וְלֹא אָכַל? אָמַר רָבָא: בְּפֵירוּשׁ רִיבְּתָה תּוֹרָה שֶׁקֶר דּוֹמֶה לְשָׁוְא, מָה שָׁוְא לְשֶׁעָבַר, אַף שֶׁקֶר לְשֶׁעָבַר.

b8.he: אֵיתִיבֵיהּ רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה לְרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ: ״שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁלֹּא אוֹכַל כִּכָּר זוֹ״, ״שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁלֹּא אוֹכְלֶנָּה״, ״שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁלֹּא אוֹכְלֶנָּה״, וַאֲכָלָהּ — אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב אֶלָּא אַחַת. וְזוֹהִי שְׁבוּעַת בִּיטּוּי, שֶׁחַיָּיבִין עַל זְדוֹנָהּ מַכּוֹת, וְעַל שִׁגְגָתָהּ קׇרְבָּן עוֹלֶה וְיוֹרֵד. זוֹהִי לְמַעוֹטֵי מַאי? לָאו לְמַעוֹטֵי ״אָכַלְתִּי״ וְלֹא ״אָכַלְתִּי״, דְּלָא לָקֵי?

b9.he: לֹא, זוֹ הִיא דְּעַל שִׁגְגָתָהּ מַיְיתֵי קׇרְבָּן, אֲבָל ״אָכַלְתִּי״ וְ״לֹא אָכַלְתִּי״ לָא מַיְיתֵי קׇרְבָּן. וּמַנִּי? רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל הִיא, דְּאָמַר: אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב אֶלָּא עַל הֶעָתִיד לָבֹא, אֲבָל מִילְקָא לָקֵי.

b10.he: אֵימָא סֵיפָא: זוֹהִי שְׁבוּעַת שָׁוְא שֶׁחַיָּיבִין עַל זְדוֹנָהּ מַכּוֹת, וְעַל שִׁגְגָתָהּ פָּטוּר. ״זוֹהִי״ לְמַעוֹטֵי מַאי? לָאו לְמַעוֹטֵי ״אָכַלְתִּי״ וְ״לֹא אָכַלְתִּי״, דְּלָא לָקֵי?

b11.he: לֹא, זוֹהִי דְּעַל שִׁגְגָתָהּ פָּטוּר מִקׇּרְבָּן, אֲבָל ״אָכַלְתִּי״ וְ״לֹא אָכַלְתִּי״ — מַיְיתֵי קׇרְבָּן. וּמַנִּי? רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא הִיא, דְּאָמַר: מְבִיאִין קׇרְבָּן לְשֶׁעָבַר.

b12.he: וְהָא אָמְרַתְּ רֵישָׁא רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל! אֶלָּא, מִדְּסֵיפָא רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא — רֵישָׁא נָמֵי רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא, וְרֵישָׁא לָאו לְמַעוֹטֵי ״אָכַלְתִּי״ וְ״לֹא אָכַלְתִּי״, אֶלָּא לְמַעוֹטֵי ״אוֹכַל״ וְלֹא אָכַל.

b13.he: וּמַאי שְׁנָא, מִשּׁוּם דְּקָאֵי בִּלְהַבָּא — מְמַעֵט לְהַבָּא, קָאֵי בִּלְהַבָּא — מְמַעֵט לְשֶׁעָבַר?

b14.he: וּמֵימֵר. אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן לְתַנָּא: לָא תִּתְנִי ״וּמֵימֵר״, מִשּׁוּם דִּבְדִיבּוּרוֹ עָשָׂה מַעֲשֶׂה.

b15.he: הַמְקַלֵּל אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ בַּשֵּׁם. מְנָלַן? אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר, אָמַר רַבִּי אוֹשַׁעְיָא: אָמַר קְרָא ״אִם לֹא תִשְׁמֹר״, וּכְתִיב ״וְהִפְלָא ה׳ אֶת מַכּוֹתְךָ״. הַפְלָאָה זוֹ אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ מַהוּ, כְּשֶׁהוּא אוֹמֵר ״וְהִפִּילוֹ הַשּׁוֹפֵט וְהִכָּהוּ לְפָנָיו״ — הֱוֵי אוֹמֵר: הַפְלָאָה זוֹ מַלְקוֹת.

b16.he: אֵימַר: אֲפִילּוּ שְׁבוּעַת אֱמֶת? בְּהֶדְיָא כְּתִיב: ״שְׁבוּעַת ה׳ תִּהְיֶה בֵּין שְׁנֵיהֶם״.

b17.he: אֵימַר הָנֵי מִילֵּי לְפַיֵּיס אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ, אֲבָל מִילְקָא לִילְקֵי? לָא מָצֵית אָמְרַתְּ, דְּהָכְתִיב ״וּבִשְׁמוֹ תִּשָּׁבֵעַ״.

b18.he: הָהוּא מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ לְכִדְרַב, דְּאָמַר רַב גִּידֵּל אָמַר רַב: מִנַּיִן שֶׁנִּשְׁבָּעִין לְקַיֵּים אֶת הַמִּצְוֹת? שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״נִשְׁבַּעְתִּי וָאֲקַיֵּמָה לִשְׁמוֹר מִשְׁפְּטֵי צִדְקֶךָ״. הָכְתִיב קְרָא אַחֲרִינָא: ״וּבוֹ תִדְבָּק וּבִשְׁמוֹ תִּשָּׁבֵעַ״.

b19.he: אֶלָּא לְמַאי אֲתָא — לִמְקַלֵּל אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ בַּשֵּׁם. וְאֵימָא — לְמוֹצִיא שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם לְבַטָּלָה? מִי גָּרַע מְקַלֵּל אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ בַּשֵּׁם מִמּוֹצִיא שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם לְבַטָּלָה?

b20.he: אֲנַן, הָכִי קָא קַשְׁיָא לַן: אֵימָא מוֹצִיא שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם לְבַטָּלָה — תִּיסְגֵּי לֵיהּ בְּמַלְקוֹת, אֲבָל מְקַלֵּל חֲבֵירוֹ בַּשֵּׁם, כֵּיוָן דְּקָעָבֵיד תַּרְתֵּי, דְּקָא מַפֵּיק שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם לְבַטָּלָה וְקָמְצַעַר לֵיהּ לְחַבְרֵיהּ — לָא תִּיסְגֵּי לֵיהּ בְּמַלְקוֹת!

messages.text: 3a

Continued from 2b: Rami bar Ḥama asked whether a Jew can effect substitution with an animal a gentile consecrated for the Jew’s atonement. The Gemara tried to resolve it from Rabbi Abbahu’s statement in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan: one who consecrates for another adds the fifth, the one achieving atonement can substitute, and one who separates teruma from his own produce…
…for the purpose of exempting the produce of another, the benefit of discretion as to which priest or Levite will receive it is his.

notes.he: של תורם שיכול ליתנו לכל כהן שירצה (אי נמי) ואם אמר לו ישראל הילך סלע זה ותנה לבן בתי כהן הוי אותו סלע של תורם ולא של נתרם בשבילו ולא מצי טעין הלה כיון שנתרמה על טבל שלו נמצא דנותן סלע על של עצמו. הך מילתא דרבי אבהו תלת מילי נינהו:
notes.en: The benefit of discretion is his: of the one separating [the teruma], who can give it to any priest he wishes. And if an Israelite said to him, “Here is this sela, and give it to my daughter’s son, a priest,” that sela belongs to the one who separated it and not to the one for whom it was separated; and the other cannot argue that since it was separated for his own untithed produce, it turns out he is being paid a sela for what is his own. This statement of Rabbi Abbahu contains three matters.

notes.he: שיכול לקבל מישראל חבירו זוז או סלע כדי ליתנה לבן בתו כהן:
notes.en: The benefit of discretion is his: for he may accept a zuz or a sela from his fellow Israelite in order to give it to his daughter’s son, a priest.

messages.text: Apparently, the halakhot of substitution follow the one achieving atonement.

There, in Rabbi Yoḥanan’s statement, the offering comes on behalf of the Jew who consecrated it. Due to that reason, we follow the one atoning, and during both the initial consecration of the offering and its ultimate sacrifice the animal is in the possession of a Jew, who is able to effect substitution.
messages.lead: Rami bar Ḥama could say to this:

notes.he: שהרי הפרישו ישראל ואהכי אזלינן בתר מתכפר דהוה ליה תחילתו וסופו ביד ישראל דאיתיה בכלל עונשין:
notes.en: There, it comes by force of an Israelite: for an Israelite set it aside. For this reason we follow the one achieving atonement, since its beginning and its end are in the hands of an Israelite, who is included in [the realm of] punishments.

notes.he: קא סבר מיהא לא תפשוט דההוא דקאמר רבי אבהו א"ר יוחנן דמתכפר עושה תמורה משום דקא אתי האי מתכפר מכח ישראל דקרבן דידיה עביד תמורה כלומר דהקדיש ישראל להתכפר ישראל. אבל הקדיש עובד כוכבים להתכפר ישראל דלא הוה מתחלה ועד סוף ברשות ההוא מתכפר מי מצי עביד מתכפר תמורה אי לא תיקו:
notes.en: And Rami bar Ḥama: holds that in any case you cannot resolve [the dilemma] from what Rabbi Abbahu said in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan, that the one achieving atonement can effect substitution. For there, this one achieving atonement comes by force of an Israelite, whose own offering can effect substitution; that is, an Israelite consecrated it for an Israelite to achieve atonement. But where a gentile consecrated it for an Israelite to achieve atonement, so that it was not in the possession of that one achieving atonement from beginning to end, can the one achieving atonement effect substitution or not? Let it stand [teiku].

messages.text: But here, where a gentile consecrated the animal, this is how he raises the dilemma: Do we require that from the initial consecration of the offering until the ultimate act of sacrifice it must be in the possession of one who is able to effect substitution or not?

notes.he: הכי גרסינן אבל הכא הכי קמיבעיא ליה מי בעינן מתחילה ועד סוף דתיקו ברשות מאן דעביד תמורה - כלומר אבל הכא בהקדיש עובד כוכבים להתכפר ישראל מי בעינן מתחילת הקדש ועד סופו שתעמוד ברשות האדם הראוי לעשות תמורה כגון ישראל והך בהמה כיון דתחילת קדושתה הויא מכח עובד כוכבים אף על גב דהוי המתכפר ישראל אינו עושה תמורה או דילמא כיון דלבסוף אתיא ביד מתכפר וחזי למיעבד תמורה תפסה בה קדושת תמורה. תיקו:
notes.en: This is the reading: “But here, this is how he raises the dilemma: Do we require from beginning to end that it stand in the possession of one who effects substitution?” That is: but here, where a gentile consecrated it for an Israelite to achieve atonement, do we require that from the beginning of the consecration to its end it stand in the possession of a person fit to effect substitution, such as an Israelite? Then this animal, since the beginning of its sanctity came by force of a gentile, cannot be substituted, even though the one achieving atonement is an Israelite. Or perhaps, since at the end it comes into the hands of the one achieving atonement, who is fit to effect substitution, the sanctity of substitution takes hold of it. Let it stand [teiku].

messages.text: The dilemma shall stand [teiku] unresolved.
§ The Master said in the baraita cited on the previous amud:
With regard to animals consecrated by gentiles, one may not derive benefit ab initio, but if one benefited from them after the fact, he is not liable for misusing consecrated property.

The halakha that one may not benefit from them ab initio is by rabbinic law. And that halakha that if one benefited from them after the fact he is not liable for misusing consecrated property is by Torah law.

notes.he: והקשה הר"ר יעקב למה לנו לומר דרבנן היא דלמא מדאורייתא היא כיון דמרבינן מאיש איש שנודרין העובדי כוכבים כישראל דכה"ג אמר (מעילה דף ז:) בשלמי ישראל דלא נהנין דאורייתא דאע"ג דאין בהן מעילה וצ"ל כיון דאין בהן קדושה לענין פיגול נותר וטמא אין בו קדושה נמי לענין הנאה דאורייתא:
notes.en: One may not benefit, by rabbinic law: Rabbi Yaakov asked: Why must we say this is rabbinic? Perhaps it is by Torah law, since we include gentiles from “any man [ish ish]” as taking vows like a Jew. For in such a case it says (Me’ila 7b), regarding the peace offerings of a Jew, that one may not benefit from them by Torah law even though they are not subject to misuse. One must say: since [gentiles’ consecrated animals] have no sanctity with regard to piggul, notar and impurity, they also have no sanctity with regard to benefit by Torah law.

notes.he: בהן מדאורייתא אפילו הכי (כי) לא נהנין מהן מדרבנן:
notes.en: One is not liable for misuse: of them by Torah law; even so, one may not benefit from them, by rabbinic law.

messages.text: What is the reason that one is not liable for misuse? As it is written with regard to misuse of consecrated property: “If anyone commit a trespass, and sin through error, in the holy items of the Lord.”

verse.he: נֶפֶשׁ כִּי־תִמְעֹל מַעַל וְחָטְאָה בִּשְׁגָגָה מִקׇּדְשֵׁי יְהֹוָה וְהֵבִיא אֶת־אֲשָׁמוֹ לַיהֹוָה אַיִל תָּמִים מִן־הַצֹּאן בְּעֶרְכְּךָ כֶּסֶף־שְׁקָלִים בְּשֶׁקֶל־הַקֹּדֶשׁ לְאָשָׁם׃
verse.en: When a person commits a trespass, being unwittingly remiss about any of GOD’s sacred things: They shall bring as a penalty to GOD a ram without blemish from the flock, convertible into payment in silver by the sanctuary weight, as a reparation offering.

messages.text: And we derive a verbal analogy from the use of the word “sin” in this verse and the word “sin” used in the context of teruma: “They shall therefore keep My charge, lest they bear sin for it” (Leviticus 22:9). And with regard to teruma it is written explicitly: “Even of all the hallowed items of the children of Israel”, from which one can infer: But not of gentiles. The halakhot of misuse as well, therefore, do not apply to animals consecrated by gentiles.

verse.he: וַיְדַבֵּר יְהֹוָה אֶל־אַהֲרֹן וַאֲנִי הִנֵּה נָתַתִּי לְךָ אֶת־מִשְׁמֶרֶת תְּרוּמֹתָי לְכׇל־קׇדְשֵׁי בְנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל לְךָ נְתַתִּים לְמׇשְׁחָה וּלְבָנֶיךָ לְחׇק־עוֹלָם׃
verse.en: GOD spoke further to Aaron: I hereby give you charge of My gifts, all the sacred donations of the Israelites; I grant them to you and to your sons as a perquisite, a due for all time.

messages.text: And if one consumes them, i.e., animals consecrated by gentiles, one is not liable for committing a transgression, with regard to the prohibitions of piggul, notar, or consuming offerings while ritually impure.

The source for this is a verse, as it is written with regard to ritual impurity: “Speak to Aaron and to his sons, that they separate themselves from the holy items of the children of Israel, which they hallow unto Me, and that they profane not My holy name”. This verse explicitly mentions items consecrated by the children of Israel, to emphasize that the halakha of distancing oneself from consecrated items while in a state of ritual impurity does not include items consecrated by gentiles.

verse.he: דַּבֵּר אֶל־אַהֲרֹן וְאֶל־בָּנָיו וְיִנָּזְרוּ מִקׇּדְשֵׁי בְנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל וְלֹא יְחַלְּלוּ אֶת־שֵׁם קׇדְשִׁי אֲשֶׁר הֵם מַקְדִּשִׁים לִי אֲנִי יְהֹוָה׃
verse.en: Instruct Aaron and his sons to be scrupulous about the sacred donations that the Israelite people consecrate to Me, lest they profane My holy name, Mine GOD’s.

messages.text: And one derives the exemption from notar by drawing a verbal analogy between the word “profane” used in the context of notar and the word “profane” used in the context of ritual impurity. As it is written in the verse cited above with regard to ritual impurity: “That they separate themselves from the holy items of the children of Israel, which they hallow unto Me, and that they profane not My holy name.”

notes.he: דבקדשי עובדי כוכבים אין בהן משום נותר:
notes.en: And he derives notar by “profane,” “profane” from impurity: that consecrated items of gentiles are not subject to [the prohibition of] notar.

notes.he: וכתב ביה בטומאה בני ישראל ולא עובדי כוכבים והקשה הר"ם ונילף נותר חילול חילול מטמא ששימש בטומאה דאמר בפרק ב' דזבחים (דף טו:) דקדשי עובדי כוכבים לא קרבי בטומאה דאמר התם אלא למעוטי עובדי כוכבים השתא ציץ לא מרצה דאמר מר בעובדי כוכבים בין בשוגג בין במזיד לא הורצה בטומאה קרב וי"ל דיש לנו למילף טפי מטומאה [דכתיב] בחד קרא כדאיתא בזבחים פ' ב"ש (זבחים דף מה:) דתני לוי מנין שאף בפסול זמן הכתוב מדבר ת"ל ולא יחללו את קדשי בני ישראל בשני חילולין הכתוב מדבר אחד פסול נותר ואחד פסול טומאה:
notes.en: And he derives notar by “profane,” “profane” from impurity: and regarding impurity it is written “the children of Israel,” and not gentiles. The Maharam asked: Let us instead derive notar by “profane,” “profane” from an impure [priest] who performed the service in impurity. For it says in the second chapter of Zevaḥim (15b) [that the exclusion of] consecrated items of gentiles [from being] offered in impurity [is unnecessary], as it says there: “Rather, to exclude gentiles? Now, the frontplate does not effect acceptance [for them], as the Master said: For gentiles, whether unwittingly or intentionally, it is not accepted; will it be offered in impurity?” One can answer: it is more fitting to derive it from impurity, [since they are written] in one verse, as is stated in Zevaḥim, chapter Beit Shammai (45b), where Levi taught: “From where [is it derived] that the verse speaks also of disqualification by time? The verse states: ‘That they not profane the holy items of the children of Israel’: the verse speaks of two profanations, one the disqualification of notar and one the disqualification of impurity.”

messages.text: And it is written with regard to notar: “But every one that eats it shall bear his iniquity, because he has profaned the holy item of the Lord”. Since the prohibition against consuming consecrated items while impure does not apply to the offerings of gentiles, neither does the prohibition of notar.

verse.he: וְאֹכְלָיו עֲוֺנוֹ יִשָּׂא כִּי־אֶת־קֹדֶשׁ יְהֹוָה חִלֵּל וְנִכְרְתָה הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַהִוא מֵעַמֶּיהָ׃
verse.en: And one who eats of it shall bear the guilt for having profaned what is sacred to GOD; that person shall be cut off from kin.

notes.dh: וכתיב גבי נותר (ויקרא י״ט:ח׳) ואוכליו עונו ישא כי את קדש ה' חלל
notes.he: מה חילול האמור גבי טומאה ישראל ולא עובדי כוכבים אף חילול האמור כאן ישראל ולא עובדי כוכבים:
notes.en: And it is written regarding notar: “But everyone who eats it shall bear his iniquity, because he has profaned the holy item of the Lord” (Leviticus 19:8): just as the profaning stated regarding impurity concerns Jews and not gentiles, so too the profaning stated here concerns Jews and not gentiles.

messages.text: And the tanna of the baraita derives the gentiles’ exemption from piggul by verbal analogy between the word “iniquity” used in the context of piggul and the word “iniquity” used in the context of notar, as it is written with regard to piggul: “And the soul that eats of it shall bear his iniquity”, and it is written with regard to notar: “But everyone that eats it shall bear his iniquity, because he has profaned the holy item of the Lord” (Leviticus 19:8).

verse.he: וְאִם הֵאָכֹל יֵאָכֵל מִבְּשַׂר־זֶבַח שְׁלָמָיו בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁי לֹא יֵרָצֶה הַמַּקְרִיב אֹתוֹ לֹא יֵחָשֵׁב לוֹ פִּגּוּל יִהְיֶה וְהַנֶּפֶשׁ הָאֹכֶלֶת מִמֶּנּוּ עֲוֺנָהּ תִּשָּׂא׃
verse.en: If any of the flesh of that sacrifice of well-being is eaten on the third day, it shall not be acceptable; it shall not count for the one who offered it. It is an offensive thing, and the person who eats of it shall bear the guilt.

messages.text: And based on these two verbal analogies, one concludes that with regard to all of them, i.e., piggul, notar, and ritually impure offerings, the prohibition against consumption applies only to offerings of the children of Israel, but not to those of gentiles.
And a gentile cannot render a non-sacred animal a substitute for one he has consecrated.

notes.dh: השתא קא מפרשינן לכולה ברייתא וקתני ואין עושין תרומה
notes.he: ומאי טעמא אין עושין תמורה:
notes.en: Now we explain the whole baraita, and it teaches: “And one does not make teruma” [the printed Rashi reads “teruma” here; the daf reads “substitution”]; and what is the reason one does not make substitution?

messages.text: As it is written with regard to substitutions: “He shall not exchange it, nor substitute it” (Leviticus 27:10), and it is written at the beginning of the matter: “Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: When a man shall clearly utter a vow of persons to the Lord, according to your valuation”. Since the passage specifically addresses the children of Israel, the halakhot of substitution apply only to them, not to gentiles.

verse.he: דַּבֵּר אֶל־בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאָמַרְתָּ אֲלֵהֶם אִישׁ כִּי יַפְלִא נֶדֶר בְּעֶרְכְּךָ נְפָשֹׁת לַיהֹוָה׃
verse.en: Speak to the Israelite people and say to them: When anyone explicitly vows to GOD the equivalent for a human being,

messages.text: Another version of the source for this halakha: The baraita states: And a gentile cannot render a non-sacred animal a substitute for one he has consecrated. What is the reason? The reason is that the substitution of consecrated animals is juxtaposed with the animal tithe (see Leviticus 27:32), and the animal tithe is juxtaposed with the grain tithe.

notes.dh: ה"ג דאיתקש תמורת בהמה למעשר בהמה
notes.he: כדאמרינן לקמן בשילהי פירקין (תמורה דף יג.) והלא מעשר בכלל שאר הקדשים וכו' למה יצא להקיש אליו ולומר לך דמה מעשר קרבן יחיד ועושה תמורה אף כל קרבן יחיד ועושה תמורה לאפוקי קרבנות צבור:
notes.en: This is the reading: “That substitution of an animal is juxtaposed with the animal tithe”: as we say below, at the end of our chapter (Temurah 13a): “But isn’t the tithe included among the other consecrated items, etc.? Why was it singled out? To juxtapose [the others] to it and tell you: just as the tithe is an individual’s offering and is subject to substitution, so too every individual’s offering is subject to substitution,” to exclude communal offerings.

notes.he: כדאמרינן בבכורות (דף נג:) עשר תעשר בשתי מעשרות הכתוב מדבר אחד מעשר בהמה ואחד מעשר דגן:
notes.en: The animal tithe is juxtaposed with the grain tithe: as we say in Bekhorot (53b): “You shall surely tithe [aser te’aser]”: the verse speaks of two tithes, one the animal tithe and one the grain tithe.

notes.dh: ל"א איתקש תמורת בהמה למעשר בהמה
notes.he: דכתיב גבי מעשר בהמה לא יבקר בין טוב לרע ולא ימירנו וכתיב בתמורת בהמה לא יחליפנו ולא ימיר אותו ומעשר בהמה איתקש למעשר דגן כדאמר בפרק מעשר בהמה עשר תעשר בשתי מעשרות הכתוב מדבר אחד מעשר דגן ואחד מעשר בהמה:
notes.en: Another version: the substitution of an animal is juxtaposed with the animal tithe: for regarding the animal tithe it is written, “He shall not inquire whether it is good or bad, neither shall he substitute it,” and regarding the substitution of an animal it is written, “He shall not exchange it, nor substitute it.” And the animal tithe is juxtaposed with the grain tithe, as it says in the chapter Ma’aser Behema: “You shall surely tithe [aser te’aser]”: the verse speaks of two tithes, one the grain tithe and one the animal tithe.

messages.text: And with regard to the grain tithe it is written: “For the tithe of the children of Israel, which they set apart as a gift to the Lord, I have given to the Levites for an inheritance”, indicating that the halakhot of the grain tithe apply only to the children of Israel, but not to gentiles. From the juxtapositions, one derives that the same holds for substitution.

verse.he: כִּי אֶת־מַעְשַׂר בְּנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲשֶׁר יָרִימוּ לַיהֹוָה תְּרוּמָה נָתַתִּי לַלְוִיִּם לְנַחֲלָה עַל־כֵּן אָמַרְתִּי לָהֶם בְּתוֹךְ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא יִנְחֲלוּ נַחֲלָה׃ {פ}
verse.en: for it is the tithes set aside by the Israelites as a gift to GOD that I give to the Levites as their share. Therefore I have said concerning them: They shall have no territorial share among the Israelites.

notes.dh: וגבי מעשר דגן כתיב (במדבר יח) כי את מעשר בני ישראל
notes.he: דמשמע בני ישראל ולא עובדי כוכבים הכי נמי גבי מעשר בהמה ישראל ולא עובדי כוכבים וכי היכי דאמרינן גבי מעשר בהמה ישראל ולא עובדי כוכבים הכי נמי נימא גבי תמורת בהמה שהרי הוקשו כולן זה לזה ומהכא נפקא דקדשי עובדי כוכבים אין עושין תמורה:
notes.en: And regarding the grain tithe it is written: “For the tithe of the children of Israel” (Numbers 18:24): which implies the children of Israel and not gentiles. So too regarding the animal tithe: Jews and not gentiles. And just as we say regarding the animal tithe, Jews and not gentiles, so too let us say regarding the substitution of an animal, since they are all juxtaposed with one another. From here it is derived that consecrated items of gentiles are not subject to substitution.

notes.he: כתיב בני ישראל ולא עובדי כוכבים והיינו רבי שמעון דאית ליה הך דרשה אבל רבנן פליגי עליה ולישנא קמא שייך לרבנן:
notes.en: And the grain tithe: it is written “the children of Israel,” and not gentiles. This is Rabbi Shimon, who holds this exposition, but the Rabbis disagree with him; and the first version belongs to the Rabbis.

messages.text: And one does not bring libations for a gentile as an independent offering, but his offering requires libations. This is the statement of Rabbi Shimon.
From where are these matters derived? They are derived from a verse, as the Sages taught in a baraita:

The verse states with regard to libations: “All that are homeborn shall do these after this manner, in presenting an offering made by fire, of a sweet savor to the Lord”. One who is homeborn, i.e., a Jew, brings libations, but a gentile does not bring libations. One might have thought that a gentile’s burnt offering should not require libations; therefore, the verse states: “So shall it be done for each bull, or for each ram, or for each of the lambs, or of the goats” (Numbers 15:10–11). This teaches that every burnt offering, even that of a gentile, requires libations.

verse.he: כׇּל־הָאֶזְרָח יַעֲשֶׂה־כָּכָה אֶת־אֵלֶּה לְהַקְרִיב אִשֵּׁה רֵיחַ־נִיחֹחַ לַיהֹוָה׃
verse.en: Every citizen, when presenting an offering by fire of pleasing odor to GOD, shall do so with them.

notes.he: זהו ישראל ולא העובד כוכבים מביא נסכים כלל:
notes.en: Homeborn: this is a Jew; and a gentile does not bring libations at all.

notes.dh: יכול לא תהא עולתו טעונה נסכים
notes.he: אפילו משל צבור:
notes.en: One might have thought that his burnt offering should not require libations: even from communal [funds].

notes.he: דככה עיכובא הוא דודאי טעונין נסכים ומשל צבור. ולל"א דכתיב בספרים ול"ג עליהן משמע הכי אזרח כגון ישראל מביא נסכים אפי' בפני עצמן ואין העובד כוכבים מביא נסכים בפני עצמן יכול לא תהא עולתו טעונה נסכים ת"ל ככה והוי עיכובא דודאי קרבנו טעון נסכים אפי' משלו דמקבלים מיניה דמי נסכים:
notes.en: The verse states “so”: for “so” indicates an indispensable requirement, that they certainly require libations, and from communal [funds]. And according to the other version, which is written in the books, and in which we do not read “for them” [in the baraita], it means this: one who is homeborn, that is, a Jew, brings libations even by themselves, and a gentile does not bring libations by themselves. One might have thought that his burnt offering should not require libations; the verse states “so,” and it is indispensable: his offering certainly requires libations, even from his own [funds], for we accept from him the money for the libations.

messages.text: I see the logic of the opinion that in all of these cases it is correct to be stringent about the offerings of gentiles.

What is the reason? With regard to the offering of a gentile, it is written: “Whosoever he be of the house of Israel, or of the strangers in Israel, that brings his offering, whether it be any of their vows, or any of their gift offerings, which are brought to the Lord for a burnt offering”. The verse equates the offerings of gentiles, “the strangers in Israel,” with those of Jews, and indicates that the consecrated status of the former is identical to that of the latter.

verse.he: דַּבֵּר אֶל־אַהֲרֹן וְאֶל־בָּנָיו וְאֶל כׇּל־בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאָמַרְתָּ אֲלֵהֶם אִישׁ אִישׁ מִבֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל וּמִן־הַגֵּר בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל אֲשֶׁר יַקְרִיב קׇרְבָּנוֹ לְכׇל־נִדְרֵיהֶם וּלְכׇל־נִדְבוֹתָם אֲשֶׁר־יַקְרִיבוּ לַיהֹוָה לְעֹלָה׃
verse.en:
Speak to Aaron and his sons, and to all the Israelite people, and say to them:
When anyone of the house of Israel, or of the strangers in Israel, presents a burnt offering as their offering for any of the votive or any of the freewill offerings that are offered to GOD,

notes.dh: ה"ג מאי טעמא לה' כתיב בהו ול"ג קדש לה'
notes.he: והכי מצאתי בזבחים בפ' ב"ש (זבחים דף מה.) מאי טעמא לה' כתיב בהו בקדשי עובדי כוכבים דכתיב איש איש מבני ישראל אשר יקריב קרבנו וגו' והאי קרא מוקמינן בעובדי כוכבים שנודרים נדרים ונדבות כישראל וכתיב בסיפיה דקרא לה' שנאמר אשר יקריב לה' לומר לך דדיינין להו בתורת שאר קדשים דמועלין בהן וחייבין עליהן משום פגול כו':
notes.en: This is the reading: “What is the reason? ‘To the Lord’ is written regarding them,” and we do not read “holy to the Lord.” So I found in Zevaḥim, in the chapter Beit Shammai (45a): “What is the reason? ‘To the Lord’ is written regarding them,” regarding consecrated items of gentiles, as it is written: “Whosoever he be of the house of Israel … that brings his offering,” etc. We establish this verse as referring to gentiles, who vow vow offerings and gift offerings like Jews; and at the end of the verse “to the Lord” is written, as it is stated: “which are brought to the Lord,” to tell you that we treat them by the law of other consecrated items: one is liable for misusing them, and one is liable for them for piggul, etc.

notes.he: דכתיב לכל נדריהם אשר יקריבו לה' הלכך מועלין:
notes.en: What is the reason? “To the Lord” is written regarding it: as it is written, “any of their vows … which are brought to the Lord.” Therefore one is liable for misusing them.

messages.text: In what case is this statement said? It is said with regard to animals consecrated for the altar, but with regard to animals consecrated for Temple maintenance, one who benefits from them is liable for misusing consecrated property.

What is the reason? The reason is that when we learn that items consecrated by gentiles are not subject to liability for misuse by the verbal analogy between the word sin and another instance of the word sin from the context of teruma, this applies only to consecrated property that is similar to teruma, which is consecrated with inherent sanctity. But with regard to an item that has the sanctity of the Temple maintenance, whose sanctity inheres in its value, as it will ultimately be sold and the proceeds used for Temple maintenance, the analogy does not apply.

notes.he: ואם תאמר והא אמר הזיד במעילה באזהרה דילפינן חטא חטא מתרומה הוה לן למימר כי הכא מה תרומה קדושת הגוף ולא יהא אזהרה דמעילה אלא בקדשי מזבח וקיימא לן דאפילו בקדשי בדק הבית שייך בהן אזהרה דמעילה כדתנן (בכריתות (דף יג:) יש אוכל אכילה אחת וחייב עליה ארבע חטאות ואשם אחד וקחשיב מוקדשים דשור וחמור) וכן כמה דרשות דרשינן בפ' בתרא דמעילה (דף יח:) פגם ונהנה ושליח שעשה שליחותו דגמרינן מתרומה היה לנו לומר דלא נהגי בקדשי בדק הבית וי"ל הא דמעטינן הכא קדשי בדק הבית היינו משום דכתיב הכא לה':
notes.en: What is teruma? Inherent sanctity: And if you say: But it is said that the warning against intentionally misusing [consecrated property] is derived by “sin,” “sin” from teruma; we should have said there, as here: just as teruma has inherent sanctity, so the warning of misuse should apply only to items consecrated for the altar. Yet we hold that the warning of misuse applies even to items consecrated for Temple maintenance, as we learned (Keritot 13b): “There is one who eats a single eating and is liable for it four sin offerings and one guilt offering,” and it counts consecrated items [there; the printed text adds a parenthetical about “an ox and a donkey” whose sense is unclear]. Likewise several expositions in the last chapter of Me’ila (18b), [about one who] damaged [an item] and benefited, and an agent who carried out his agency, which we derive from teruma; we should have said that they do not apply to items consecrated for Temple maintenance. One can answer: the reason we exclude items consecrated for Temple maintenance here is that “to the Lord” is written here.

messages.caption: The baraita on animals consecrated by gentiles, ruling by ruling, with the source the Gemara gives for each.

messages.text: With regard to any prohibition in the Torah, if one performed an action to transgress it, he is liable to receive lashes. But if he did not perform an action to transgress it, he is exempt from receiving lashes.
messages.lead: § The mishna teaches that one who effects substitution receives lashes. Rav Yehuda says that Rav says:

messages.text: But is it an established principle that one who transgresses a prohibition that does not involve an action is exempt? But there is the prohibition of substitution, which is a prohibition that does not involve an action, and one is flogged for transgressing it, as we learned in the mishna:
messages.quote: if he did not perform an action to transgress it, he is exempt

notes.dh: והרי מימר דלאו שאין בו מעשה הוא
notes.he: דבדיבורא תליא מילתא:
notes.en: But there is substitution, which is a prohibition that does not involve an action: for the matter depends on speech.

notes.dh: והרי מימר לאו שאין בו מעשה ולקי
notes.he: ואם תאמר אמאי לא פריך הכי נמי ממוציא שם רע ועדים זוממין דלאו שאין בו מעשה ולקי וי"ל דלא בעי למיפרך מהני דכתיב בהו מלקות בתורה וא"ת במסכת מכות (דף ד:) דאמר עולא לאו שאין בו מעשה לוקין עליו דיליף ממוציא שם רע ופריך מה למוציא שם רע שכן קנס ולימא או נשבע או מימר או חד מהנך דשמעתין [יוכיח] וי"ל דאין ה"נ אלא תירץ שפיר או שמא לא דמי הני דהכא להני דהתם ואם תאמר כי פריך הכא והרי מימר דלאו שאין בו מעשה לימא בדיבוריה איתעביד מעשה כדאמר לקמן וי"ל דאה"נ הוי מצי לתרוצי אלא דשפיר שני:
notes.en: But there is substitution, a prohibition that does not involve an action, and he is flogged: And if you say: Why does it not likewise challenge from one who defames [his bride] and from conspiring witnesses, whose prohibitions do not involve an action, and one is flogged? One can say: it did not want to challenge from those, since lashes are written explicitly for them in the Torah. And if you say: In Tractate Makkot (4b), where Ulla says one is flogged for a prohibition that does not involve an action and derives it from one who defames, the Gemara challenges: “What about one who defames? He is [also subject to] a fine.” Let it say: one who takes an oath, or one who effects substitution, or one of the others in our passage will prove [the point]. One can say: it is indeed so, but the answer given [there] is also sound; or perhaps the cases here are not similar to those there. And if you say: When the Gemara challenges here, “But there is substitution, which is a prohibition that does not involve an action,” let it answer that through his speech an action was done, as it says below. One can say: it indeed could have answered so, but the answer it gave is also sound.

messages.text: That is not to say that it is permitted for a person to effect substitution; rather, it means that if one substituted a non-sacred animal for a consecrated animal, the substitution takes effect, and the one who substituted the non-sacred animal incurs the forty lashes.

In accordance with whose opinion is this mishna written? It is in accordance with that opinion of Rabbi Yehuda, who said: With regard to a prohibition that does not involve an action, one is flogged for transgressing it. The Rabbis, however, disagree.

notes.he: דקא משתעי לקמן בהא מילתא:
notes.en: It is Rabbi Yehuda: who discusses this matter below.

messages.text: But can you establish the mishna as being in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda? But we established the first clause of the mishna as not being in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda, as it teaches: Everyone substitutes a non-sacred animal for a consecrated animal, and the Gemara added (2a): What does the expansive term everyone serve to include? It serves to include an inheritor, and accordingly, this mishna is not in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that an inheritor cannot effect substitution.

The tanna of this mishna holds in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda with regard to one matter, that one is flogged for transgressing a prohibition that does not involve an action, and disagrees with him with regard to one other matter.

As Rabbi Yehuda holds that an inheritor does not place his hands on the head of the offering when he sacrifices it, and an inheritor is not able to substitute a non-sacred animal for a consecrated one that he inherited; and the tanna of our mishna holds that an inheritor places his hands on the head of the offering when he sacrifices it, and an inheritor is able to substitute a non-sacred animal for a consecrated one that he inherited.

With regard to every prohibition in the Torah, if one performed an action to transgress it, he is flogged. But if he did not perform an action to transgress it, he is exempt from lashes, except for one who takes an oath, and one who effects substitution, and one who curses another using the name of God. For these three transgressions, even though he did not perform an action, he is liable to receive lashes.
messages.lead: Rav Idi bar Avin says that Rav Amram says that Rabbi Yitzḥak says that Rabbi Yoḥanan says in the name of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili:

notes.dh: לא עשה מעשה פטור חוץ מנשבע כו'
notes.he: דאע"ג דלא עביד מעשה לוקה כדמפרש להו לקמן:
notes.en: If he did not perform an action he is exempt, except for one who takes an oath, etc.: for they are flogged even though they perform no action, as is explained below.

notes.he: בשמו של הקב"ה:
notes.en: Using the name: using the name of the Holy One, Blessed be He.

notes.he: הקדש. וכן המקדים תרומה לבכורים לא במפריש קא מיירי דהיינו מעשה שהקדיש תרומה אלא כגון שנתן עיניו בצד זה לשם תרומה. אימא לא ינקה כלל אפי' ב"ד:
notes.en: And one who curses another using the name: [the name] of the Holy [One]. And likewise one who separates teruma before the first fruits: this does not refer to one who actually separates it, which would be an action of consecrating teruma, but, for example, to one who set his eyes on this side [of the produce] as teruma. [On 3b:] Say that he is not cleared at all, even by the court.

messages.text: Also one who separates teruma prior to designating the first fruits is flogged, even though teruma can be separated by intention alone, without an action.
messages.lead: They said in the name of Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina:

notes.he: לקמן מפרש טעמא דאמר קרא מלאתך ודמעך לא תאחר מלאתך זו בכורים ודמעך זו תרומה ואמר רחמנא לא תאחר ובספרי מפרש טעמא אחרינא יקדמו בכורים שיש להן ד' שמות ורש"י מייתי ליה לקמן (תמורה ד' ד. ד"ה מפני):
notes.en: Also one who separates teruma before the first fruits: below (4a) it explains the reason, that the verse states: “You shall not delay to offer of your fullness and of your outflow” [Exodus 22:28]: “your fullness” is the first fruits, and “your outflow” is teruma, and the Merciful One said, “You shall not delay.” The Sifrei explains another reason: the first fruits should come first, since they have four names. Rashi cites it below (Temurah 4a, s.v. mipnei).

messages.text: From where do we derive that one who takes an oath using the name of God is flogged?
messages.quote: except for one who takes an oath

notes.he: דלוקה:
notes.en: One who takes an oath, from where do we derive: that he is flogged?

messages.text: The verse states: “For the Lord will not hold him guiltless that takes His name in vain”. One can infer: The higher, i.e., heavenly, court…

verse.he: לֹא תִשָּׂא אֶת־שֵׁם־יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ לַשָּׁוְא כִּי לֹא יְנַקֶּה יְהֹוָה אֵת אֲשֶׁר־יִשָּׂא אֶת־שְׁמוֹ לַשָּׁוְא׃ {פ}
verse.en: You shall not swear falsely by the name of the ETERNAL your God; for GOD will not clear one who swears falsely by that name.

messages.text: 3b
…does not hold him guiltless, as repentance alone will not atone for the sin, but the lower, i.e., earthly, court flogs him, thereby allowing him to atone, and absolves him of guilt.

notes.he: דכתיב כי לא ינקה ה':
notes.en: They do not clear him: as it is written, “For the Lord will not clear him.”

messages.text: @Abaye But why not say that the verse means he cannot be absolved of guilt at all?

notes.he: דאין מלקין אותו בית דין שלמטה:
notes.en: [He cannot be absolved] at all: that the lower court does not flog him [to clear him].

messages.text: If so, let the verse write only: “Will not hold him guiltless,” and be silent. Why do I need the verse to specify: “For the Lord will not hold him guiltless”? This serves to teach that it is the higher court that will not hold him guiltless, but the lower court flogs him and absolves him of guilt.
messages.quote: he cannot be absolved of guilt at all

messages.text: § We found a source for the halakha that one who takes an oath in vain using the name of God is flogged. From where do we derive that the same holds for a false oath?

notes.he: דכתיב (שמות כ׳:ז׳) אשר ישא את שמו לשוא והיינו שבועת שוא כגון נשבע לשנות את הידוע לאדם:
notes.en: We found an oath in vain: as it is written, “that takes His name in vain” (Exodus 20:7); this is an oath in vain, such as one who swears to alter what is known to people.

notes.he: מפרש לקמן היכי דמי:
notes.en: A false oath: it explains below what the case is.

notes.he: דלקי עלה:
notes.en: From where do we derive it: that he is flogged for it?

notes.he: דלקי שבועת שוא היינו נשבע לשנות את הידוע לאדם אמר על עמוד של אבן שהוא של זהב או נשבע אם לא ראיתי נחש כקורת בית הבד:
notes.en: We found an oath in vain: that he is flogged. An oath in vain is one who swears to alter what is known to people: he said of a stone pillar that it is of gold, or swore [that he saw something absurd, such as]: “If I did not see a snake like the beam of an olive press.”

messages.text: The verse states with regard to an oath taken in vain: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain; for the Lord will not hold him guiltless that takes His name in vain”. It says: “In vain…in vain,” twice in this verse. If the second instance of the term is not necessary for the matter of an oath taken in vain, which is derived from the first instance, apply it to the matter of a false oath, to teach that one who takes such an oath is flogged.

verse.he: לֹא תִשָּׂא אֶת־שֵׁם־יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ לַשָּׁוְא כִּי לֹא יְנַקֶּה יְהֹוָה אֵת אֲשֶׁר־יִשָּׂא אֶת־שְׁמוֹ לַשָּׁוְא׃ {פ}
verse.en: You shall not swear falsely by the name of the ETERNAL your God; for GOD will not clear one who swears falsely by that name.

messages.text: What are the circumstances of the false oath under discussion? If we say that the one taking the oath said: I take an oath that I will not eat a certain item, and he then ate that item; there he performed an action to violate his oath by eating the item, and the prohibition would then involve an action.
messages.lead: Rabbi Abbahu objects to this explanation of Rabbi Yoḥanan:
messages.quote: apply it to the matter of a false oath

notes.he: ובדין הוא דלילקי שהרי אכל ועשה מעשה:
notes.en: He performed an action: and by right he should be flogged, since he ate and so performed an action.

messages.text: And if it was rather a case where he said: I take an oath that I will eat a certain item, and he did not eat that item; is that individual flogged? But wasn’t it stated: If one says: I take an oath that I will eat this loaf today, and the day passed and he had not eaten it, Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish both say: He is not flogged.

notes.he: דלאו היינו מעשה:
notes.en: And he did not eat: for this is not an action.

notes.he: בתמיה:
notes.en: Is that individual flogged?: said in astonishment.

messages.text: He is not flogged, as it is a prohibition that does not involve an action, and one is not flogged for any prohibition that does not involve an action.

He is not flogged, as there was only an uncertain forewarning for the transgressor. One must be warned immediately before the transgression to be held liable, but here there was no single moment of transgression, and one is not flogged for any transgression that follows an uncertain forewarning.

notes.he: דאי אתרו ביה הזהר בך שתאכל הככר שנשבעת עליה יכול לומר אין לי בית מיחוש בהתראה זו דאכתי יש לי שהות וכן כל היום כולו ואפי' כי עבר היום יכול לומר שוכח הייתי ולא נזכרתי לא בשבועה ולא בהתראה ואינו לוקה:
notes.en: Because it is an uncertain forewarning: for if they warn him, “Take care to eat the loaf about which you swore,” he can say, “This warning gives me no cause for concern, as I still have time,” and so all day long. And even when the day has passed he can say, “I forgot, and remembered neither the oath nor the warning,” and he is not flogged.

notes.he: שכשמתרין בו היזהר שתאכלנה היום הוא אומר כן אעשה כשאהיה פנוי ועדיין יש שהות הרבה ביום ואם עבר היום ולא אכלה יכול לומר שכחתיה דכל התראה שאינה בשעת מעשה כגון זו הוי התראת ספק ולא שמה התראה שיכול לומר שכחתי ההתראה:
notes.en: Because it is an uncertain forewarning: for when they warn him, “Take care to eat it today,” he says, “I will do so when I am free, and there is still much time in the day”; and if the day passed and he did not eat it, he can say, “I forgot it.” For any forewarning that is not at the time of the act, such as this one, is an uncertain forewarning and is not considered a forewarning, since he can say, “I forgot the warning.”

messages.text: If Rabbi Yoḥanan holds he is not flogged, to what case is he referring when he states that one is flogged for a false oath even though no action is involved?

Let the case be where one says: I take an oath that I ate a certain item, and in fact he did not eat it; or he said: I take an oath that I did not eat a certain item, and in fact he did eat it. In these cases, he transgresses the prohibition by speech alone, without an action.

notes.he: כלומר תהא שבועת שקר בנשבע שלא אכל ואכל או שאכל ולא אכל דהכא ליכא שום מעשה דהא לשעבר נשבע:
notes.en: Let it be with “I ate” or “I did not eat”: that is, let the false oath be where one swore that he did not eat and he had eaten, or that he ate and he had not eaten. Here there is no action at all, since he swore about the past.

notes.he: דלקי על שבועת שקר דאמר שבועה שאכלתי ולא אכל או שבועה שלא אכלתי ואכל קודם השבועה וההוא דקודם השבועה לא הוה מעשה:
notes.en: Rather, Rabbi Abbahu said: let it be: that he is flogged for a false oath where he said, “An oath that I ate,” and he had not eaten, or, “An oath that I did not eat,” and he had eaten before the oath; and what was before the oath is not an action [connected to the oath].

messages.text: And what is different about an oath concerning the past, that the verse includes one who takes an oath of: I ate, or: I did not eat, as liable to be flogged, more than one who takes an oath of: I will eat, and then did not eat? In both cases, there is no action performed.

notes.he: כלומר מאי איריא דקא ממעט אוכל ולא אכל ממלקות טפי מאכלתי ולא אכלתי הא בתרוייהו ליכא שום מעשה:
notes.en: And what is different about “I ate” or “I did not eat”: that is, why specifically does it exclude “I will eat” and he did not eat from lashes, more than “I ate” or “I did not eat”? In both there is no action at all.

notes.he: באוכל ולא אוכל דאמרת כיון דלית ביה מעשה לא לקי ומ"ש באכלתי ולא אכלתי דאמרת אע"ג דלית ביה מעשה לקי:
notes.en: And what is different: with “I will eat” and he did not eat, you said that since it involves no action he is not flogged; and what is different with “I ate” or “I did not eat,” that you said that although it involves no action he is flogged?

messages.text: The Torah explicitly includes a case of a false oath that is similar to a case of an oath taken in vain: Just as an oath taken in vain refers to the past, so too, the false oath for which one is flogged must pertain to the past.

notes.he: כדמפקא לעיל לשוא לשוא שתי פעמים:
notes.en: A false oath similar to an oath in vain: as was derived above from “in vain,” “in vain,” twice.

notes.he: דכי נשבע על עמוד של אבן שהוא של כסף היינו לשעבר דלשעבר קודם שנשבע הויא אבן כמו שהיא עכשיו ומה שוא לוקה עליה כדאמרי' לעיל בב"ד שלמטה מלקין ומנקין אותו אף שקר לשעבר דהיינו אכלתי ולא אכלתי לאפוקי אוכל ולא אכל שהוא להבא:
notes.en: Just as an oath in vain is about the past: for when one swears about a stone pillar that it is of silver, that is about the past, since in the past, before he swore, it was a stone, as it is now. And just as for an oath in vain he is flogged, as we said above, “the lower court flogs him and clears him,” so too a false oath about the past, that is, “I ate” or “I did not eat,” to exclude “I will eat” and he did not eat, which concerns the future.

notes.he: שבועת שקר דכתיב לשוא לשוא תרי זימני הלכך בעינן שקר דומה [לשבועת] שוא (דשוא לשעבר שנשבע בחנם) [מה שוא לשעבר שנשבעין לשנות את הידוע לאדם ואמר על עמוד של אבן שהוא של זהב כו' (היינו באכלתי ולא אכלתי)] ומכזב על מה שעבר שהוא יודע לשעבר שאינו כן אף שקר נמי בעינן לשעבר היינו אכלתי ולא אכלתי [דלשעבר הוא:
notes.en: The Torah explicitly included: a false oath, as it is written “in vain,” “in vain,” twice. Therefore we require a false oath similar to an oath in vain: just as an oath in vain is about the past, where one swears to alter what is known to people, saying of a stone pillar that it is of gold, and lies about what has passed, knowing that it was not so, so too for a false oath we require one about the past, that is, “I ate” or “I did not eat,” which concerns the past. [The printed text of this note carries several bracketed corrections; this rendering follows the corrected reading.]

messages.text: If one says: I take an oath that I will not eat this loaf; I take an oath that I will not eat it; I take an oath that I will not eat it, and he then ate it, he is liable for only one violation. And this is the oath of an utterance for which one is liable to receive lashes for its intentional violation, and to bring a sliding-scale offering for its unwitting violation.
messages.lead: Rabbi Yirmeya raised an objection to Rabbi Abbahu from a mishna:

notes.dh: שבועה שלא אוכל ככר זו וכו'
notes.he: דהא נשבע תלת זימני שלא יאכל אותו ככר:
notes.en: An oath that I will not eat this loaf, etc.: for he swore three times that he would not eat that loaf.

notes.he: כדאמרינן בשבועות דאין שבועה חלה על שבועה:
notes.en: He is liable for only one: as we say in Shevuot that an oath does not take effect upon an oath.

notes.he: דקאמר קרא לבטא בשפתים להרע או להיטיב וגו' וזו היא שבועת ביטוי שמוציא בשפתיו שלא יאכל אותו ככר אבל לא גזיל מידי לחבריה אבל שבועת העדות ושבועת הפקדון מביא על הזדון כשגגה אשם:
notes.en: And this is the oath of utterance: of which the verse says, “to utter with the lips, to do evil or to do good” (Leviticus 5:4). This is the oath of utterance: he utters with his lips that he will not eat that loaf, but he did not rob his fellow of anything. But for the oath of testimony and the oath of deposit, one brings [an offering] for intentional violation as for unwitting violation: a guilt offering [for the oath of deposit].

notes.dh: שבועה שלא אוכל ככר זו שבועה שלא אוכלנה ואכלה אינו חייב אלא אחת
notes.he: ודוקא נקט שבועה שלא אוכל תחילה דאי אמר שבועה שלא אוכלנה שבועה שלא אוכל חייב שתים דשלא אוכלנה משמע כולה וכי הדר אמר שבועה שלא אוכל משמע כלל ובשבועות (דף כז:) מפרש אמאי תנא שלא אוכלנה שני פעמים:
notes.en: An oath that I will not eat this loaf, an oath that I will not eat it, and he ate it, he is liable for only one: It specifically put “an oath that I will not eat” first. For had he said, “An oath that I will not eat it,” and then, “An oath that I will not eat,” he would be liable for two: “that I will not eat it” implies the whole of it, and when he then says, “An oath that I will not eat,” it implies [not eating] at all [even a little]. And in Shevuot (27b) it explains why it teaches “that I will not eat it” twice.

notes.he: דאין שבועה חלה על שבועה:
notes.en: He is liable for only one: for an oath does not take effect upon an oath.

messages.text: When the mishna uses the limiting term: This is the oath, what does it serve to exclude? Is it not to exclude a case where one said: I take an oath that I ate a certain item, when in fact he did not eat it, or: I take an oath that I did not eat a certain item, when he did eat it, to teach that he is not flogged in those cases? This would contradict the explanation of Rabbi Abbahu.

notes.he: דאין חייבין על זדונה מכות:
notes.en: To exclude what?: that one is not liable to lashes for its intentional violation.

notes.he: דאע"ג דהויא שבועת ביטוי דלא לקי משום דלהרע או להיטיב כתיב דמשמע להבא פרט לשעבר כגון אכלתי ולא אכלתי ואכתי שבועת שקר היכי דמי:
notes.en: Is it not to exclude “I ate” or “I did not eat”?: that although it is an oath of utterance, he is not flogged, since “to do evil or to do good” is written, which implies the future, excluding the past, such as “I ate” or “I did not eat.” And [if so,] what then is the case of the false oath?

messages.text: No, in both cases one is flogged for violating the prohibition intentionally. Rather, the phrase means: This is the oath for which one brings an offering for its unwitting violation, but in a case where one unwittingly said: I ate a certain item, when he in fact did not eat it, or: I did not eat a certain item, when he did eat it, he does not bring an offering.

notes.he: משום דלהרע או להיטיב גבי קרבן קאי אבל ממה נפשך חייב עליה מלקות דומיא דשבועת שוא:
notes.en: He does not bring an offering: because “to do evil or to do good” is stated with regard to the offering; but in any case he is liable to lashes for it, similar to an oath in vain.

notes.he: אבל אכלתי ולא אכלתי לא מייתי קרבן אלא לקי:
notes.en: But “I ate” or “I did not eat”: he does not bring an offering, but he is flogged.

messages.text: And whose opinion does this mishna represent? It is the opinion of Rabbi Yishmael, who said: One is liable to bring an offering only for an oath that refers to the future, but one is flogged even for an oath that pertains to the past.

notes.he: [ר"י] במס' שבועות (דף כה.) אינו חייב אלא על העתיד לבא:
notes.en: Who said: [Rabbi Yishmael,] in Tractate Shevuot (25a): one is liable only for the future to come.

messages.text: But say the latter clause of the mishna:

If one takes an oath that a stone is gold or some similar absurdity, this is the oath taken in vain, for which one is liable to receive lashes if he utters it intentionally and for which one is exempt from bringing an offering if he utters it unwittingly.

notes.he: סיפא דההיא משנה דלעיל הויא האי זו היא שבועת שוא וכו':
notes.en: This is an oath in vain: this “This is an oath in vain, etc.” is the latter clause of that mishna cited above.

messages.text: What does the limiting term: This is the oath, used by the mishna serve to exclude? Does it not serve to exclude a case where one said: I ate a certain item, when he in fact did not eat it, or: I did not eat a certain item, when he did eat it, to teach that he is not flogged in those cases?

No, in both cases one is flogged for violating the prohibition intentionally. Rather, the phrase means: This is the oath for which one is exempt from bringing an offering if he utters it unwittingly, but in a case where one said: I ate a certain item, when he in fact did not eat it, or: I did not eat a certain item, when he did eat it, he brings an offering.

notes.he: אבל אכלתי ולא אכלתי מייתי קרבן ולקי:
notes.en: But “I ate” or “I did not eat”: he brings an offering, and he is flogged.

messages.text: And whose opinion does this represent? It is the opinion of Rabbi Akiva, who said: One brings an offering even for the violation of an oath that refers to the past.
But didn’t you say earlier that the first clause represents the opinion of Rabbi Yishmael, that one does not bring an offering for a false oath pertaining to the past?

Rather, from the fact that the latter clause represents the opinion of Rabbi Akiva, it follows that the first clause must represent the opinion of Rabbi Akiva as well. And one must therefore suggest an alternative explanation of the first clause. The phrase: This is the oath, employed there does not, as previously claimed, serve to exclude a case where one said: I ate a certain item, or: I did not eat a certain item. Rather, it serves to exclude a case where one said: I will eat a certain item, and he did not subsequently eat it.

notes.dh: ורישא לאו למעוטי אכלתי ולא אכלתי
notes.he: דאכלתי ולא אכלתי ודאי חייב על שגגתה קרבן:
notes.en: And the first clause is not to exclude “I ate” or “I did not eat”: for “I ate” or “I did not eat” he is certainly liable to an offering for its unwitting violation.

notes.dh: ורישא לא למעוטי אכלתי ולא אכלתי מקרבן אלא למעוטי אוכל ולא אכל
notes.he: מקרבן:
notes.en: And the first clause is not to exclude “I ate” or “I did not eat” from an offering, but to exclude “I will eat” and he did not eat: from an offering.

messages.text: And what is different about an oath pertaining to the future, that the mishna should exclude it specifically?

notes.he:
דממעט אוכל ולא אכל מקרבן וקא מרבי אכלתי ולא אכלתי מסיפא דחייב קרבן:
ומשני מסתברא רישא למעוטי אוכל ולא אכל:
notes.en: And what is different: that it excludes “I will eat” and he did not eat from an offering, while it includes “I ate” or “I did not eat,” from the latter clause, as liable to an offering? It answers: it stands to reason that the first clause excludes “I will eat” and he did not eat.

notes.he: פרש"י מאי שנא דממעט אוכל ולא אכל מקרבן וקמרבי אכלתי ולא אכלתי מסיפא דחייב בקרבן ולא נהירא דאי אמר למעוטי אוכל ולא אכל לא קשיא מידי אבל אי אמר איפכא אז תיקשה לך ור"י פירש ומאי שנא דמפרש לה כרבי עקיבא לוקמא כר' ישמעאל ורישא למעוטי אכלתי ולא אכלתי מקרבן וסיפא למעוטי אוכל ולא אכל ממלקות ומשני קאי בלהבא כו':
notes.en: And what is different: Rashi explained: what is different, that it excludes “I will eat” and he did not eat from an offering, and includes “I ate” or “I did not eat,” from the latter clause, as liable to an offering? This is not clear: if it says that it excludes “I will eat” and he did not eat, there is no difficulty at all; only if it had said the reverse would there be a difficulty. The Ri explained: what is different, that it explains [the mishna] according to Rabbi Akiva? Let it establish it according to Rabbi Yishmael, with the first clause excluding “I ate” or “I did not eat” from an offering and the latter clause excluding “I will eat” and he did not eat from lashes. And it answers: since it deals with the future, etc.

notes.he: דהאי ממעט]:
notes.en: And what is different: that this one excludes [the future].

messages.text: Since this clause of the mishna deals with an oath that pertains to the future, it stands to reason that it would exclude an oath pertaining to the future. If it deals with an oath that pertains to the future, why would it exclude an oath pertaining to the past?

notes.he: דקתני שבועה שלא אוכלנה וממעט להבא כגון אוכל ולא אכל:
notes.en: Since it deals with the future: for it teaches “an oath that I will not eat it,” and it excludes the future, such as “I will eat” and he did not eat.

notes.he: בתמיה. כגון אכלתי ולא אכלתי:
notes.en: But if it deals with the future, would it exclude the past?: said in astonishment; for example, “I ate” or “I did not eat.”

notes.he: בשבועה שלא אוכל ממעט להבא שבועה שאוכל ולא אכל אבל אכלתי דלשעבר הוא לא ממעט אלא לקי (עליה) וכדר' אבהו:
notes.en: Because it deals with the future: with “an oath that I will not eat,” it excludes the future, an oath “that I will eat” and he did not eat. But “I ate,” which concerns the past, it does not exclude; rather, he is flogged for it, in accordance with Rabbi Abbahu.

messages.text: In summary, the entire mishna is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Akiva. The first clause excludes from the punishment of lashes the passive violation of an oath pertaining to the future, and the latter clause includes in the obligation to bring an offering a false oath pertaining to the past if he uttered it unwittingly. Neither clause contradicts the explanation of Rabbi Abbahu.

messages.caption: Which oaths bring lashes for intentional violation and an offering for unwitting violation, as the Gemara works them out.

messages.text: § In listing those who incur the punishment of lashes even though they did not perform an action in their transgression, Rabbi Yosei HaGelili was cited above as including: And one who effects substitution.
Do not teach: And one who effects substitution, in this regard, because one who effects substitution performs an action of consecration by his speech.
messages.lead: Rabbi Yoḥanan said to the tanna who would recite the baraitot in his academy:

notes.he: בכלל שאר לאוין שאין בהן מעשה:
notes.en: Do not teach “and one who effects substitution”: among the other prohibitions that do not involve an action.

notes.he: שעושה מחולין קדשים:
notes.en: For by his speech he performs an action: for he makes non-sacred [animals] into consecrated ones.

notes.he: שמקדיש בהמת חולין. ליראה את השם קס"ד דהאי ליראה את השם היינו שתירא אותו שלא תקלל בו חבירו וכתיב ביה הפלאה דהיינו מלקות:
notes.en: Because by his speech he performed an action: for he consecrates a non-sacred animal. “That you may fear this name”: it enters our mind that this “that you may fear the name” means that you should fear it so as not to curse your fellow with it, and hafla’a is written regarding it, which is lashes.

messages.text: § Rabbi Yosei HaGelili also lists one who curses another using the name of God as liable to be flogged. From where do we derive this?
messages.quote: one who curses another using the name

notes.he: אם לא תשמור לעשות והפלא ואזהרתיה מהכא לא תקלל חרש אי נמי מהאי קרא גופיה:
notes.en: And one who curses another using the name, from where do we derive it: “If you will not observe to perform … then [the Lord] will make wondrous.” Its warning is from here: “You shall not curse the deaf”; alternatively, from this verse itself.

messages.text: The verse states: “If you will not observe to perform all the words of this law that are written in this book, that you may fear this glorious and awesome name, the Lord your God”. This refers to one who curses using the name of God. And it is written immediately thereafter: “Then the Lord will make your plagues wondrous [vehifla]” (Deuteronomy 28:59).

verse.he: אִם־לֹא תִשְׁמֹר לַעֲשׂוֹת אֶת־כׇּל־דִּבְרֵי הַתּוֹרָה הַזֹּאת הַכְּתֻבִים בַּסֵּפֶר הַזֶּה לְיִרְאָה אֶת־הַשֵּׁם הַנִּכְבָּד וְהַנּוֹרָא הַזֶּה אֵת יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ׃
verse.en: If you fail to observe faithfully all the terms of this Teaching that are written in this book, to reverence this honored and awesome Name, the ETERNAL your God,

notes.he: עד ליראה את השם שיתיירא שלא להוציא את השם לבטלה וכן מקלל את חבירו בשם מוציאו לבטלה וכתיב והפלא ה' את מכותך שיטול מכות והיינו מלקות:
notes.en: If you will not observe to perform, etc.: up to “that you may fear the name,” that he should fear not to utter the name in vain; and one who curses another using the name likewise utters it in vain. And it is written, “Then the Lord will make your plagues wondrous,” that he will receive blows, and that is lashes.

messages.text: With regard to this term hafla’a, I do not know what its meaning is. When it says: “And the judge shall cause him to lie down [vehippilo] and to be beaten before him”, you must say that the term hafla’a is referring to lashes.

verse.he: וְהָיָה אִם־בִּן הַכּוֹת הָרָשָׁע וְהִפִּילוֹ הַשֹּׁפֵט וְהִכָּהוּ לְפָנָיו כְּדֵי רִשְׁעָתוֹ בְּמִסְפָּר׃
verse.en: if the guilty one is to be flogged, the magistrate shall have them lie down and shall supervise the giving of lashes, by count, as warranted by the offense.

messages.text: Why not say that even one who utters a true oath is flogged, as this too could be considered exhibiting insufficient fear of God’s name?

notes.he: דקא מזהר קרא דאפילו שבועת אמת לא ליעבד בשם שמים ואי עביד והפלא ה' את מכותך שיטול מלקות:
notes.en: Even a true oath: that the verse warns that one should not make even a true oath with the name of Heaven, and if he does, “Then the Lord will make your plagues wondrous,” that he receives lashes.

notes.he: אימא האי ליראה את השם אינו מקלל את חבירו בשם אלא שתירא אותו שלא תהא נשבע בשמו אפילו באמת]:
notes.en: Say that this “that you may fear the name” is not about one who curses another using the name, but that you should fear it so as not to swear by His name, even truthfully.

messages.text: It is written explicitly that a bailee may take an oath in court, as the verse states: “The oath of the Lord shall be between them both, to see whether he has not damaged his neighbor’s goods”.

verse.he: שְׁבֻעַת יְהֹוָה תִּהְיֶה בֵּין שְׁנֵיהֶם אִם־לֹא שָׁלַח יָדוֹ בִּמְלֶאכֶת רֵעֵהוּ וְלָקַח בְּעָלָיו וְלֹא יְשַׁלֵּם׃
verse.en: an oath before GOD shall decide between the two of them that the one has not laid hands on the property of the other; the owner must acquiesce, and no restitution shall be made.

notes.he: דשרי למיעבד:
notes.en: It is written explicitly: that it is permitted to do so.

messages.text: Why not say that this statement in the verse means only that a bailee is able to appease the other, i.e., the owner, and exempt himself from payment for the damaged goods, but he should nevertheless be flogged?

notes.he: שלא יהא תובעו ממון אבל מילקא לילקי הואיל ומביא עצמו לידי שבועה:
notes.en: To appease his fellow: so that he will not claim money from him; but he should be flogged, since he brings himself to an oath.

notes.he: אימא האי שבועת ה' תהיה בין שניהם לאו שיהא מותר לכתחילה לישבע באמת אלא משום הכי צריך שבועה כדי להפיס דעתו של בעל הבית ואימא ומוטב שיפיס דעתו בממון ולא בשבועה ואם לא רצה ממון אלא שבועה ישבע לו כדי להפיס דעתו אבל ילקה על (שבועתו של) [שבועה] אמת ואימא להכי הוא דאתא ליראה את השם ולא למקלל חברו בשם:
notes.en: Say that this “The oath of the Lord shall be between them both” does not mean that it is permitted ab initio to swear truthfully. Rather, an oath is needed in order to appease the mind of the owner. And say: it is better that he appease him with money and not with an oath, and if [the owner] does not want money but an oath, he swears to him to appease him, but he is flogged for the true oath. And say that this is what “that you may fear the name” comes for, and not for one who curses another using the name.

messages.text: You cannot say this, as it is written: “You shall fear the Lord your God, and Him you shall serve, and by His name you shall swear”. This verse clearly indicates that it is permitted to take a truthful oath using the name of God.

verse.he: אֶת־יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ תִּירָא וְאֹתוֹ תַעֲבֹד וּבִשְׁמוֹ תִּשָּׁבֵעַ׃
verse.en: Revere only the ETERNAL your God; worship [God] alone; swear only by God’s name.

notes.he: דשבועת אמת שריא למעבד:
notes.en: And by His name you shall swear: that it is permitted to make a true oath.

messages.text: Isn’t that verse required as a source for the halakha of Rav?

notes.he: דעל שבועת אמת ילקה דהא כתיב קרא אחרינא דשרי דכתיב ובשמו תשבע אימא ההוא ובשמו תשבע דשרי לאישתבע לא שרי אלא לדבר מצוה משום לזרוזי נפשיה וכדרב גידל אמר רב:
notes.en: That you cannot say: that he is flogged for a true oath, for another verse is written that permits it, as it is written, “and by His name you shall swear.” [The Gemara answers:] Say that “and by His name you shall swear,” which permits swearing, permits it only for a matter of a mitzva, in order to spur himself on, in accordance with what Rav Giddel said that Rav said.

messages.text: From where is it derived that it is permitted for one to take an oath obligating himself to fulfill the mitzvot? It is derived from a verse, as it is stated: “I have sworn, and have confirmed it, to observe Your righteous ordinances”.

verse.en:
I have firmly sworn
to keep Your just rules.

notes.he: כדי שלא יוכל לחזור בו שנאמר נשבעתי ואקיימה וגו' ואהכי איצטריך האי קרא ובשמו תשבע לאשמועינן דנשבע לקיים את המצוה מותר:
notes.en: To fulfill the mitzvot: so that he cannot retract, as it is stated, “I have sworn, and have confirmed it,” etc. And for this the verse “and by His name you shall swear” is needed, to teach us that one who swears to fulfill a mitzva is permitted to do so.

messages.text: There is another source: Isn’t another verse written: “You shall fear the Lord your God; Him you shall serve; and to Him you shall cleave, and by His name you shall swear”. This second verse teaches that it is permitted for one to take a truthful oath.

verse.he: אֶת־יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ תִּירָא אֹתוֹ תַעֲבֹד וּבוֹ תִדְבָּק וּבִשְׁמוֹ תִּשָּׁבֵעַ׃
verse.en: You must revere the ETERNAL your God—whom you shall worship, to whom you shall hold fast, and by whose name you shall swear.

notes.he: דתרי קראי כתיבי ובשמו תשבע חד בואתחנן וחד בוהיה עקב חד מיבעי ליה דנשבע לקיים את המצוה ואידך לשבועת אמת:
notes.en: But another verse is written, “and by His name you shall swear”: two verses are written with “and by His name you shall swear,” one in [the portion of] Va’etḥanan and one in Ekev. One is needed for one who swears to fulfill a mitzva, and the other for a true oath.

notes.he: הא כתב קרא אחרינא ובשמו תשבע דתרי זימני כתיב ובשמו תשבע [חד לכדרב גידל] וחד למישרי אפילו שבועת אמת דעלמא ואייתר ליה ליראה את (ה') למקלל חברו בשם:
notes.en: But another verse is written, “and by His name you shall swear”: for “and by His name you shall swear” is written twice, [one for the teaching of Rav Giddel] and one to permit even an ordinary true oath; and so “that you may fear” remains free for one who curses another using the name.

notes.he: ל"א ההוא דרב גידל מן ובו תדבק נפקא [אלא ובשמו תשבע למה לי אם אינו ענין לשבועת הדיינים דמותרת דנפקא מן שבועת ה' תניהו ענין לשבועה דעלמא לאו דדיינין ואם אינו ענין לשבועה דמצוה דנפקא מן ובו תדבק תניהו ענין לשבועת אמת דחול ליראה את השם כו']:
notes.en: Another version: that teaching of Rav Giddel is derived from “and to Him you shall cleave.” [Then why do I need “and by His name you shall swear”? If it is not needed for the oath of judges, which is permitted and is derived from “the oath of the Lord,” apply it to an ordinary oath that is not before judges; and if it is not needed for an oath for a mitzva, which is derived from “and to Him you shall cleave,” apply it to a true oath (it seems it should read: a true oath that is optional). If so, this verse “that you may fear the name” perforce comes for one who curses another.]

messages.text: The Gemara resumes the discussion of one who curses another: Rather, the term vehifla in Deuteronomy 28:59 comes to teach what? It comes to teach that one who curses another using the name of God is flogged.

notes.he: האי אם לא תשמור וגו':
notes.en: Rather, for what does it come: this “If you will not observe,” etc.

notes.he: דודאי לקי אע"ג דלא עביד מעשה:
notes.en: For one who curses another using the name: that he is certainly flogged, even though he performed no action.

messages.text: But why not say that that verse refers to one who pronounces the name of Heaven in vain? Even if it does, is cursing another using the name of God any less of a sin than pronouncing the name of Heaven in vain? If one is flogged for the latter, certainly one is flogged for the former.

notes.he:
אבל מקלל את חבירו בשם לא לקי:
ומהדר ליה לאו כל דכן הוא:
notes.en: The name of Heaven in vain: but one who curses another using the name would not be flogged. And it answers him: is it not all the more so?

notes.he: ואימא האי ליראה לחייב למוציא שם [שמים] לבטלה הוא דאתא ולא למקלל:
notes.en: And say that this “that you may fear” comes to make one who utters the name [of Heaven] in vain liable, and not one who curses.

messages.text: This is what is difficult for us: One can say that for one who pronounces the name of Heaven in vain, it is sufficient for him to receive lashes to atone for his act, but in the case of one who curses another using the name of God, since he has performed two improper acts, first that he pronounces the name of Heaven in vain, and second that he inflicts pain on another, it should not be sufficient for him to receive lashes to atone for his act.

notes.dh: דהיכא דקא עביד תרי איסורי לא תיסגי ליה במלקות
notes.he: ואף על גב דלקה אפילו הכי לא נתכפר עדיין במלקות לחודיה:
notes.en: For where he commits two prohibitions, lashes should not suffice for him: and even though he was flogged, he has still not been atoned for through lashes alone.

notes.he: האי לא מצית אמרת דמי גרע מקלל את חברו בשם ממי שמוציא שם שמים לבטלה דהא מקלל (את חבירו) בשם תרי איסורי עביד דמוציא שם לבטלה לקלל את חברו ועוד שמקלל חבירו ודאי לא גרע (ממוציא שם שמים) [אלא חמיר] (אנן הכי מצינו למימר) אנן הכי קא קשיא לן דנימא מוציא שם שמים לבטלה תיסגי ליה במלקות דנימא דלהכי כתיב והפלא. אבל מקלל את חברו בשם לא תיסגי ליה במלקות דתרתי עביד:
notes.en: This you cannot say: for is one who curses another using the name any less than one who utters the name of Heaven in vain? For one who curses using the name commits two prohibitions: he utters the name in vain in order to curse his fellow, and moreover he curses his fellow; he is certainly not less, [but more severe]. This is what is difficult for us: let us say that for one who utters the name of Heaven in vain, lashes suffice for him, and that is why “make wondrous” is written; but for one who curses another using the name, lashes should not suffice, since he did two [things].

messages.text: Continues on 4a: the Gemara answers from “You shall not curse the deaf”: if the verse is about cursing another, that is the source of its warning, but for pronouncing God’s name in vain, where would the warning come from?
